query: Which method can be used for high-temperature oxidation behaviour and phase stability, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Using in situ high‐temperature X‐ray diffraction (HTXRD) enables the accurate observation of oxidation behavior and phase stability in high‐entropy alloys by directly tracking the formation and transformation of phases in real time during heating.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast or homogenized CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) with a stable single-phase FCC structure at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to controlled high-temperature conditions (in air and/or vacuum) while continuously recording XRD patterns with the in situ HTXRD setup.
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidation experiments conducted over a temperature range spanning from below 750 °C up to above 800 °C (or higher as needed), in both oxidizing and inert atmospheres.
generation.structural_mediator: The emergence, shift, and/or disappearance of specific diffraction peaks indicating the onset of oxide formation (e.g., non-protective Mn oxides) or phase decomposition (such as FCC to sigma or spinel phases).
generation.mechanism: As the alloy is heated, oxidation reactions and phase transformations occur; the in situ HTXRD captures these changes in real time by detecting new diffraction peaks or changes in existing ones, thereby correlating the time–temperature history with phase evolution.
generation.predicted_outcome: Distinct differences in the XRD patterns will appear as temperature increases, such as the emergence of diffraction peaks from oxidized species or new phases, which aligns with thermodynamic predictions from CALPHAD approaches. This will demonstrate HTXRD’s effectiveness in resolving time-dependent phase formation and oxidation behavior.
generation.baseline: Ex situ measurements that may miss transient phases or underestimate the kinetics of the oxidation process, leading to less accurate correlation of phase stability with temperature.
generation.boundary: The resolution of HTXRD might be limited in detecting very minor or amorphous phases; thus, some subtle oxidation products might not be observed, and overlapping peaks may obscure phase identification in complex systems.
generation.uncertainty: While HTXRD is expected to capture prominent phase transformations, uncertainties remain regarding its detection limits for minor or rapidly transient phases, and the influence of experimental parameters (such as heating rate and atmosphere) on the results.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct an in situ HTXRD experiment on a CrMnFeCoNi HEA sample under a controlled high-temperature oxidation process. Monitor and record the XRD patterns continuously as the temperature is elevated in both oxidizing and inert atmospheres. Compare the detected phase changes against predictions from thermodynamic calculations (e.g., CALPHAD).
measurements: Continuous XRD pattern collection to identify peak emergence, shifts, or disappearance
Temperature profiles and atmosphere control records
Quantitative analysis of phase fractions over time
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the in situ HTXRD does not clearly capture the expected onset and progression of oxide formation or phase transformations (e.g., if expected diffraction peaks do not emerge or differ significantly from thermodynamically predicted behavior), then the hypothesis that HTXRD provides an accurate, time-resolved measure of high-temperature oxidation behavior and phase stability in HEAs would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions.
